function.name: generate_sea_foam
function.description: Simulates the creation of sea foam based on the agitation level of water, amount of organic material, and the presence of salt. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

agitation_level.description: The level of agitation in the water, represented by a scale from 1 (calm) to 10 (very agitated).

organic_material.description: The amount of organic material present in grams per liter. This is a float type value.

salt_presence.description: Indicates whether salt is present (true) or not (false) in the water.

temperature.description: The water temperature in degrees Celsius. If unspecified, defaults to average sea temperature. This is a float type value.

message.content:
The sea typically looks blue—especially when it’s clear and calm—because water absorbs longer wavelengths (red, orange, yellow) more strongly than shorter wavelengths (blue). When sunlight hits the surface, the shorter blue wavelengths scatter in all directions, giving the ocean its characteristic hue.

However, the exact shade can change depending on several factors:

| Factor | Effect on Color |
|--------|-----------------|
| **Depth** | Deeper water scatters less light, often appearing darker or even blackish. |
| **Algae & phytoplankton** | High concentrations give the water a greenish tint. |
| **Sediment & runoff** | Suspended particles can make the water brown or murky. |
| **Sun angle & weather** | Low sun angles or overcast skies can produce a grayish or turquoise appearance. |
| **Reflection of sky** | A bright, cloudless sky can enhance the blue look; a stormy sky may darken it. |

So while “blue” is the common shorthand, the sea’s color is actually a dynamic blend of physics, biology, and environmental conditions.
